rows.34:0d2c:
...First, shall I introduce myself?
My name is Akemi Iwashita.
I'm in Class 3-A.
...So the seventh one never came after all.
Did they forget? Or did some problem keep them from coming?
...Or were they never invited in the first place?
I suppose none of that matters.
Whatever the reason, the fact is they aren't coming.
Fate can't be changed, can it?
...But is fate truly something that can't be changed?
Some people say a person's fate is entirely decided from the moment they're born.
That God has decided every human being's fate.
And that no matter how you struggle, it can never be changed.
Some people preach that all people are equal, but I don't think so.
Some are born rich, and some are born poor.
And plenty of them stay exactly that way until the day they die.
Is that equality?
I don't think it is.
If that is what fate is, then God is cruel, isn't he?{p}Tell me, {a}{f:|}.
Do you believe in fate?
rows.34:10d4:
I see, so you believe in fate.
Do you think that fate can be changed?
rows.34:1138:
...Heh heh.
I'm gradually starting to see what kind of person you are.{p}
rows.34:1174: ...Well then, are you satisfied with your life?
rows.34:11d0:
I see.
So you're happy.
But is that true satisfaction?
You might have been able to lead a far more wonderful life.
If you ask me, I think you're settling.
If you want to win true happiness, you have to seize it, even if it means killing others.{p}
rows.34:1328:
Even if you try to change your fate, it won't change easily.
You have to struggle for it: hard work, study, self-control.
Even then, if such a thing as fate exists, I can't imagine it changing easily.
...But you know, there is an easy way.
At least, a way that leaves the person themselves satisfied.
Can you guess what it is?
Relying on objects.
It's very common these days, isn't it?
Power stones, tachyon goods, pyramid power.
Things of that sort, said to hold supernatural powers.
By relying on such things, people try to change their fate and carve out a bright future.
What comes of leaning entirely on outside powers without making any effort...
Anyone with a brain should know that already.
{a}{f:|}, isn't there someone like that around you?
Someone who's become obsessed with that sort of mysterious power.
There's one in my class.
A pitiful person who has fallen under the spell of that kind of magic.{p}
rows.34:1658:
Her name is Yuriko Okawa.
Okawa was especially interested in power stones.
Power stones are stones that hold mysterious powers; to put it simply, crystals.
There are many kinds of stones, and each has a different effect.
Your eyesight improves, illnesses are cured, your mind is calmed, money piles up; things like that happen just from having the stone.
Sounds like a dream, doesn't it?
Of course, some people say such things are unrealistic.
But if the people who want to believe choose to believe, that's their right.
If having a power stone puts someone in the right frame of mind, I'd say that alone makes it worth plenty.
One famous power stone is lapis lazuli.
They say if you carry it, you can find happiness.
Lost things turn up, loves you thought were hopeless come true.
It also holds the power to turn bad luck around.
Perhaps those are trivial things that would happen whether you had lapis lazuli or not.
But what people choose to think is up to them.
It was even a bit of a fad among girls at one point{f:, you know| - you must remember}.
But among enthusiasts, there's a rumor of a lucky power stone with effects beyond even lapis lazuli.{p}
rows.34:1ab8:
Its name is Rubelize.
Rubelize is a beautiful amber-colored stone, but apparently it's extremely rare.
It's all but impossible to get in Japan, and it's not priced so that ordinary people can easily buy it.
Even so, they say Rubelize's power is tremendous.
They say it grants its owner's every wish, whatever that wish may be.
But it's a strange story, isn't it?
If you could afford something as expensive as Rubelize, I think most of your wishes would come true anyway.
And still wanting Rubelize on top of that... how stupid.
I can't understand the way rich people think.{p}
rows.34:1cc4:
And of course, Okawa knew about Rubelize too.
She had lapis lazuli, but that alone was no longer enough for her.
That's human greed for you.
Once she learned that Rubelize existed, she could no longer believe in lapis lazuli's power.
But Rubelize cost more than she could ever obtain in her whole life, no matter how hard she worked.
She would have had to sacrifice her happiness just to get the stone of happiness.
But she was the type to rely on outside powers in the first place, wasn't she?
People like that are selfish.
When they can't get what they want, they want it all the more.
So she apparently prayed to God every day.
"Dear God.
Please, I beg you, grant me Rubelize.
I'll do anything."
...How stupid.
If she had time for that, she should have spent it working hard instead.{p}
rows.34:1fac:
But it's a strange thing.
Maybe God really does exist.
Her wish was granted.
Though it all began with a rumor that didn't ring very true.{p}
rows.34:2064:
She happened to overhear some classmates talking.
"Hey, hey, do you know about Rubelize?"
"What's that?"
Okawa wanted to join the conversation right away.
But she kept a straight face and just listened in.
"It's a really expensive power stone, but it works amazingly well."
"Ooh, I want one."
"Don't be stupid.
You can't just buy one that easily.
...But you know, apparently a senior at our school had one a long time ago."
"Wow... amazing."
Okawa was stunned and listened intently.
To think someone at this very school had owned Rubelize...
Okawa was so envious and so frustrated she felt her heart would burst.{p}
rows.34:22c0:
"...But you know, that person died."
"Whaaat!
Then you can't count on that stone's power at all.
If the owner died, it was a fake, I bet."
"I don't think so.
I mean, they died in an accident.
Up until then they were super happy, apparently."
"Really?"
"Really.
And then they buried it in that person's grave with them.
That Rubelize."
"What a waste!"
Okawa couldn't hold back any longer.
She hurried to join the conversation.{p}
rows.34:2494:
"Hey!
What was that senior's name?"
"...I think it was Okazaki... Okazaki... um, I don't know the first name, but I'm pretty sure it was Okazaki."
That was all Okawa needed to know.
The rest she could find out by looking into it.
All she had to do was find an Okazaki who had been a student at this school and died young.{p}
rows.34:25d4:
When she went through the old graduation albums, she found Okazaki right away.
Her full name was Yukie Okazaki.
She had been a student about twenty-five years before Okawa.
That Okazaki had known about Rubelize so long ago, and had even owned it, made Okawa hate her bitterly.
Back then, power stones weren't even something ordinary people talked about.
That's just how selfish people are.{p}Naturally, you can guess what Okawa had in mind, can't you?
rows.34:2768: Ask Okazaki's parents to let her have it
rows.34:278c: Dig up Okazaki's grave and steal it
rows.34:27c4:
...That's right.
That's just the sort of thing Okawa would think of.
By then, there was nothing in her head but Rubelize.
And she had already convinced herself it was hers.
So she couldn't stand that her property was stored away in someone else's grave.
And she decided she had to go and take it back.
What kind of nerve does it take to convince yourself of something like that?{p}
rows.34:2924: Okawa hurried to the grave where Okazaki slept, trying to calm her racing heart.{p}...Tell me, before I go on with this story, wouldn't you like to know what kind of person this Okazaki was?
rows.34:29e8: ...Then I'll tell you Yukie Okazaki's story.{p}
rows.34:2a3c:
Okazaki, you see, was apparently the daughter of a powerful zaibatsu family.
And when her father went abroad, he got hold of a Rubelize.
They say even at the prices back then it cost as much as a house, so as casual souvenirs from abroad go, it was far beyond anything people like us could imagine.
She liked the stone very much.
At the time, nobody yet cared that it was a stone that brought happiness.
It was simply rare even by world standards, so apparently it became the talk of the school.
And the girls who told Okawa about her must have heard that rumor from somewhere too.
Okazaki was a fine pianist.
She'd been given elite piano training since before she could even remember.
It had apparently been settled that she would go study in Europe.
Back then, studying abroad wasn't a dream ordinary people could make come true, so it was a big deal.
Even so, she hated the idea.
She loved Japan, so she didn't want to leave.
So, on the condition that she would become the pianist her parents wanted, she was allowed to stay in Japan just for high school.
Her parents naturally pushed for a prestigious girls' school.
Even so, she wanted an ordinary high school life.
In that sense, I suppose she was a young lady with far more sense than her parents.{p}
rows.34:2eb4:
And so she came here.
But this school didn't have much in the way of facilities.
There was a grand piano, of sorts, but it was hardly the kind of thing that would satisfy her parents.
So they ordered the finest one from Rome and donated it to the school.
The school was delighted.
The grand piano in the music room of the new school building today is that very one.
But Okazaki wasn't pleased.{p}
rows.34:3024:
And she was drawn more to an old organ sleeping in a corner of the old school building than to that grand piano.
The organ had been left abandoned, covered in dust, unused.
Even so, for some reason, she found that organ captivating.
Back then, there was no new school building yet.
Most classes were held in the old school building.
As far as the school was concerned, they'd been given that magnificent grand piano, after all.
So they gave her permission to use the organ all to herself.
Nobody was using it anyway.{p}
rows.34:31ec:
After school, wherever you were, you could hear the sound of her playing the organ.
They say it was a warm melody, more soothing to the heart than the grand piano was, no matter who played it.
The story goes that many students stayed at school after hours, doing nothing in particular, just to hear that melody.
No one knows why she was drawn to that organ.
Still, they say that when she laid her fingers on the keys, the organ's sound came alive, as if life had been breathed into it.
And the more she played that organ, the more she felt that she truly loved music.
But at the same time, her desire to study in Europe kept fading away.
And she wished that, if at all possible, she would never have to go to Europe.{p}
rows.34:3460:
Around that time, Okazaki had the Rubelize her father gave her made into a necklace.
Today you'd call it a pendant that brings happiness, I suppose.
And every time she wished, I don't want to go to Europe, I don't want to go, she clutched that pendant tight.
As if she were praying to the Rubelize.{p}Well, {a}{f:|}?
You've prayed to God or some divine being before too, haven't you?
rows.34:35e8:
I thought so.
Most Japanese people today are atheists, yet they pray to God only when they're in trouble.
Without even specifying which god.
Even though there are so many gods in the world.
Did you know?
Devils are gods too.
So whoever grants your wish might be a devil, not a god.
Heh heh...
Well, to people who worship devils, they're perfectly respectable gods.{p}
rows.34:3854:
One day, while she was playing the organ as usual, the key cover suddenly slammed shut.
With tremendous force, though there was no wind at all.
It was just like a devil's mouth.
In the instant the cover came plunging down, it must have looked to her like a savage beast with sharp fangs.
The people who had been entranced by her melody were startled, wondering what had happened.
Suddenly, they heard a scream that seemed to echo up from the depths of hell.{p}
rows.34:39fc:
Everyone rushed to her side.
And there they witnessed a tragic accident.
The organ's cover was shut, as if it had closed its mouth.
Red blood was dripping from the gap, like drool.
And she lay collapsed beside it.
Her hands were stained bright red.
When the person who helped her up took her hands, both index fingers were gone, snapped clean off at the base.
When they opened the cover, her two fingers were resting gently on the keys.
She was operated on right away.
Maybe because not much time had passed, they somehow managed to reattach her fingers.
But she could never move them the way she used to.
She could live a normal life, but that brilliant playing was utterly, utterly beyond her...
They say it was a crushing blow.
Not so much to her as to her parents.{p}
rows.34:3cd0:
But with this, her wish came true.
She no longer needed to study abroad.
In exchange, her dream of being a pianist was shattered, too.
Even so, she could still gather children and teach them piano.
For her, opening a little classroom and playing piano with children seemed more fun than traveling the world as a pianist.{p}
rows.34:3f28:
Once she was discharged and could go back to school, the very first thing Okazaki did was go to see that organ.
She didn't bear the organ any grudge.
After all, it was an accident.
No one was to blame.
An unlucky thing that just happened by chance.
But when she went to the music room, she was stunned.
The organ was gone.
She pressed the teacher about where the organ had gone.
The teacher hedged at first, reluctant to say, but finally gave in to her pushing and let it slip.
That the organ had been sold off somewhere far away, at her father's wish.{p}
rows.34:4218:
I don't need such a horrible father anymore.
That's what she thought.
Clutching that pendant that brought happiness.
And she thought this, too:
I want to see that organ once more.
I want to go to where that organ is.{p}
rows.34:42e8:
Thinking such things, she wandered out of the school in despair, unsteady on her feet.
And she was hit in a traffic accident.
She was struck by an oncoming car and killed instantly.
They say even after she breathed her last, she was still clutching the pendant that brought happiness.
That Rubelize power stone.
This came out afterward, but by then the organ was already gone from this world.
On her father's orders, the organ hadn't been sold; it had been destroyed.
The teacher couldn't bear to say so and lied that it had been sold.
But that lie led to her death.
The organ went to heaven, and she followed after it, to where the organ was.
I wonder if she's playing the organ in heaven now.
For the angels who died young...{p}
rows.34:4588:
And the pendant she held to the very end was laid in the Okazaki family grave along with her remains.
They say her father grieved terribly.
And not long after, he fell ill and departed this world, as if his daughter had beckoned him.
Her wish came true.
The Rubelize granted her wish.
I'm sure she was happy.{p}
rows.34:46f0:
...Well?
Do you understand Rubelize's power now?
rows.34:4800:
Finding out where Okazaki's grave was posed no difficulty at all.
She'd go to the Okazaki home and say she was a junior from Okazaki's school, that she'd happened to hear the story, and that she'd very much like to visit the grave.
Say that, and they'd hardly refuse.
They'd kindly tell her, without suspecting a thing.
And she did exactly that.
Okawa waited until late at night, then made her move.{p}
rows.34:4958:
Graveyards are frightening even in the daytime, I think.
And this was the middle of the night.
A high school girl, all alone.
That's not something just anyone could do.
And her purpose was grave robbing, no less.
Okawa must have had nerves of steel.
Or maybe the Rubelize sleeping in the grave called her to it.
Heh heh...
In any case, she moved the gravestone aside and took Okazaki's urn out from inside.
And when she opened the urn... there it was.{p}
rows.34:4af8:
A beautiful amber pendant.
"Mine!
It's my Rubelize!"
She clutched it and hugged it to her chest.
Now I can be happy...
I'll be happier than anyone, happier than absolutely anyone.{p}Well, {a}{f:|}?
Now that Okawa had her Rubelize, do you think she found happiness?
rows.34:4ce8:
But she did become happy.
It was a world apart from Okazaki's case.
It couldn't be helped, after all.
In Okazaki's case, she didn't know Rubelize was a power stone that brings happiness, did she?
So she didn't know how to use it.
It just happened to hear her wish, that's all.
But Okawa's case was different.
Even if it was a devil's stone, she didn't use it the wrong way.
So there was no way she wouldn't be happy.{p}
rows.34:4e8c:
First, she got a wonderful sweetheart.
She was fairly pretty, so that's no surprise.
She could have found a sweetheart without the stone's help.
But there are quite a lot of people like that.
People who normally can't do a thing, yet whose personality suddenly changes from a little self-suggestion.
Okawa was one of those.
The self-suggestion of owning the Rubelize stone made her confident about everything.
But what happens when that goes too far...
Not knowing is a frightening thing.{p}
rows.34:506c:
She broke it off right away.
She'd finally found a wonderful sweetheart, but it wasn't enough for her.
She had the Rubelize.
So she deserved an even more wonderful sweetheart.
Put simply, she got bored.
When she asked the stone, the breakup came right away.
Though as arrogant as she'd become, the breakup would have come soon enough without asking the stone.
She got money, too.
A huge insurance payout.
Her father died, and the insurance money came to her.
Nobody suspected that she had killed him.
In fact, they actually felt sorry for her.
What fools, all of them.
She grew happier and happier.
As her wishes came true.{p}
rows.34:52b4:
But her heart was never truly satisfied.
After all, she was always chasing the greatest happiness.
There was no way she could be satisfied.
And so she thought:
I'm unhappy.
She had the Rubelize, so why couldn't she be happy? The frustration became unbearable.
Then she thought of a good way.
And she asked the stone.
Can you guess what that wish was?
It's simple.
After all, she couldn't be happy herself.{p}
rows.34:544c:
She clutched the Rubelize and said this:
"Please, make everyone unhappy."{p}
rows.34:54b8:
......Do you see?
Right now, her wish is in the middle of coming true.
And I'm sure that wish will never be satisfied either.
And she'll surely keep on asking.
"Make everyone more and more unhappy."
That's what she'll ask.{p}

notes: 34:3f28/42e8: the teacher's gender unstated; no pronouns used.
